subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Ozone Hole Discovery
description: A quick win: understand The Ozone Hole Discovery.

hook.text: In 1985, scientists in Antarctica found something terrifying: the ozone layer had a hole.

buildup.text: CFCs from fridges and spray cans were destroying ozone molecules in the stratosphere.

discovery.text: Within two years, 197 nations signed the Montreal Protocol and banned CFCs entirely.

twist.text: It worked. The ozone hole has been slowly shrinking since the late 1990s.

climax.text: This remains the most successful global environmental treaty ever signed.

punchline.text: The world can fix the sky — when it agrees to try.

quiz.question: When was the ozone hole discovered?

details.summary: British scientists discovered the Antarctic ozone hole in 1985 using ground-based instruments at Halley Station. NASA satellites had recorded the depletion but software had flagged the extreme values as errors. The discovery shocked the world and led to the Montreal Protocol.
details.whyItMatters: The ozone hole discovery shows how political boundaries cannot contain atmospheric problems and how scientific evidence can drive swift international action.
takeaways: CFCs released chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone
The hole appears each Antarctic spring over the South Pole
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased out ozone-depleting substances

faq.question: Is the ozone hole recovering?
faq.answer: Yes, but slowly. Because CFCs persist in the atmosphere for decades, the ozone layer is not expected to fully recover until around 2066 over Antarctica. However, the rate of depletion has clearly reversed thanks to the Montreal Protocol.

faq.question: Why does the ozone hole form specifically over Antarctica?
faq.answer: Extreme cold during the Antarctic winter creates polar stratospheric clouds that provide surfaces for chemical reactions releasing chlorine from CFCs. When spring sunlight returns, this chlorine rapidly destroys ozone, creating the annual hole.
